a: I live as a stranger in Meshech
p: The Hebrew names Meshech, a far northern people. The Greek and both Latin Psalters read "has been prolonged."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Targum, which reads a people's name ("the Asians")
readings.plain: I live as a stranger in Meshech

readings.w: Old Greek (Codex Sinaiticus in Swete's edition, Vaticanus being lost here; Alexandrinus and the Verona and Zurich Psalters do not differ) (Psalm 119:5); Gallican Psalter incolatus meus prolongatus est; Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew peregrinatio mea prolongata est
readings.plain: my stay among strangers has dragged on

why: The consonants mshk can be the name Meshech or the verb mashakh, "draw out." The Hebrew pairs Meshech, a people of central Anatolia far to the north, with Kedar, a tribe of the north Arabian desert to the south-east: the speaker feels surrounded by strangers. The Greek reading, which even Jerome kept in his Psalter from the Hebrew, fits the next verse ("I have lived far too long") and may have been chosen because Meshech seemed impossible for a Judean. The Plain keeps the name, which makes the harder and more vivid picture.

a: they are ready for war.
p: The Greek and the Gallican Latin add "they fought me without cause."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew et illi bellantia
readings.plain: they are ready for war.

readings.w: Old Greek (Codex Sinaiticus in Swete's edition, Vaticanus being lost here; Alexandrinus and the Verona and Zurich Psalters do not differ) (Psalm 119:7); Gallican Psalter inpugnabant me gratis
readings.en: they made war on me without cause
readings.plain: they made war on me without cause.

why: The Hebrew is terse: "I, peace; and when I speak, they, for war." The Greek fills it out with a verb and the word dōrean, "for nothing, without cause," the word John 15:25 uses for "they hated me without cause" (from 35:19 or 69:4). The Greek also joins the first half to the previous verse: "with those who hate peace I was peaceable." The shorter Hebrew is followed.

a: Of David.
p: The Hebrew and Sinaiticus name David; Alexandrinus and other Greek copies leave the name out.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Codex Sinaiticus (Swete's edition, Psalm 121:0); the Great Psalms Scroll from Cave 11, 11QPs-a (11Q5); Gallican Psalter huic David; Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew David
readings.plain: Of David.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus, the Verona Psalter (R) and the Zurich Psalter (T), from Swete's apparatus

why: Four Songs of Ascents name David in the Hebrew (122, 124, 131, 133) and one Solomon (127). The Greek copies do not agree on these names (see the note on 124:0); for 122 the omission is in Alexandrinus and two Psalters, while Sinaiticus, the Qumran scroll and the Latin keep it. The Hebrew is followed. On whether David could have written of the tribes going up to the LORD's house, see the chapter page.

a: the contempt of the proud.
p: The written text has one word, "the proud"; the margin reads two words, "the proud ones of the oppressors."

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Ketiv (the written consonants); Old Greek tois hyperēphanois (Psalm 122:4)
readings.plain: the contempt of the proud.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Qere (the reading in the margin), Leningrad Codex
readings.plain: the contempt of proud oppressors.

why: The scribes wrote lg'ywnym as one word, a rare form of "proud" (ga'ayon). The Masoretes' marginal reading splits it into ge'ei yonim, "the proud of the oppressors," or, as later Jewish readers heard it, "the proud of the Greeks" (Yevanim). The Greek supports the single word. The Plain follows the written text, which keeps the parallel with "the comfortable."

a: we were like people dreaming.
p: The Hebrew says "dreaming"; the Greek and the Gallican Latin say "comforted."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew quasi somniantes
readings.plain: we were like people dreaming.

readings.w: Old Greek (Codex Sinaiticus in Swete's edition, Vaticanus being lost here; Alexandrinus and the Verona and Zurich Psalters do not differ) (Psalm 125:1); Gallican Psalter sicut consolati
readings.plain: we were like people comforted.

readings.w: Targum (Aramaic paraphrase)
readings.en: like the sick who are healed
readings.plain: we were like people made well.

why: The Greek and the Targum may both take cholmim from the second root chalam, "be strong, healthy" (Isaiah 38:16): "made well," and so "comforted." "Dreaming" is the common sense of the word and fits the wonder of the return. The Plain follows it.

a: Of Solomon.
p: The Hebrew names Solomon; the Greek text in Swete's edition has no name.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); the Great Psalms Scroll from Cave 11, 11QPs-a (11Q5); the Verona Psalter (R); Gallican Psalter and Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew Salomonis
readings.plain: Of Solomon.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus (Swete's edition, Psalm 126:0)

why: The Verona Psalter and both Latin Psalters have Solomon's name, so some Greek copies had it. The name fits the psalm's "house" and "beloved" (see the notes on 127:0 and 127:2). The Hebrew is followed.

a: Across my back the plowmen plowed;
p: The Hebrew has plowmen cutting furrows; the Greek has sinners working on my back, prolonging their lawlessness.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew super cervicem meam arabant arantes
readings.plain: Across my back the plowmen plowed;

readings.w: Old Greek (Codex Sinaiticus in Swete's edition, Vaticanus being lost here; Alexandrinus and the Verona and Zurich Psalters do not differ) (Psalm 128:3); Gallican Psalter supra dorsum meum fabricabantur peccatores
readings.orig: ἐπὶ τοῦ νώτου μου ἐτέκταινον οἱ ἁμαρτωλοί
readings.en: on my back the sinners were working
readings.plain: Across my back the sinners did their work;

readings.w: The Great Psalms Scroll from Cave 11, 11QPs-a (11Q5)
readings.en: on my back the wicked plowed
readings.plain: Across my back the wicked plowed;

why: The verb charash means both "plow" and "work, engrave, devise" (as a craftsman or a plotter). The Greek took the second sense and turned the image into a moral statement. In the second half the Hebrew "furrows" (ma'anitam, with a Ketiv and Qere difference in spelling) became "lawlessness" in the Greek. The Qumran scroll keeps the verb "plowed" but, like the Greek, names the attackers "the wicked" (resha'im, the word of 129:4) instead of "plowmen" (chorshim), a one-letter shift that makes the same moral point. The Hebrew picture of the whip-scarred back is followed.

a: so that people will stand in awe of you.
p: The Hebrew says forgiveness leads to awe. The Greek has "for your name's sake"; the Gallican, "for your law."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew cum terribilis sis
readings.en: so that you may be feared
readings.plain: so that people will stand in awe of you.

readings.w: Old Greek: Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and the Zurich Psalter (Swete's edition, Psalm 129:4)
readings.plain: for your name's sake.

readings.w: The Verona Psalter (R) nomou, from Swete's apparatus; Gallican Psalter propter legem tuam
readings.plain: for the sake of your law.

why: The Greek translator joined this half verse to the next ("for your name's sake I waited for you, LORD"), and Greek copies differ between "name" and "law": the Verona Psalter and the Gallican Latin have "law," and the first hand of Sinaiticus has "his law" in verse 5 instead of the Hebrew "his word." The Qumran fragment 4QPs-e (4Q87) agrees with the Hebrew. "Feared" (tiwwarē') is the harder thought, that mercy produces reverence, and the Greek may have softened it. The Hebrew is followed. In 130:6 the Greek and Latin also read "from the morning watch until night."

a: My soul lies on me like that weaned child.
t: "Like a weaned child," or "so you would repay"?
p: The Hebrew ends with the soul at rest like a weaned child; the Greek ends an oath: "so may you repay my soul."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew ita ablactata ad me anima mea
readings.en: like the weaned child upon me (is) my soul
readings.plain: My soul lies on me like that weaned child.

readings.w: Old Greek (Codex Sinaiticus in Swete's edition, Vaticanus being lost here; Alexandrinus and the Verona and Zurich Psalters do not differ) (Psalm 130:2); Gallican Psalter ita retributio in anima mea
readings.orig: ὡς ἀνταποδώσεις ἐπὶ τὴν ψυχήν μου
readings.en: so you would repay upon my soul
readings.plain: So may you pay back my soul.

why: The Greek read the oath form "if not" ('im lo') as a full curse: "If I was not humble-minded but lifted up my soul ... so may you repay my soul." The last word gamul ("weaned") is the same root as gamal, "deal out, repay" (137:8), which explains the Greek. The Hebrew image of the quiet child is followed.

a: all the pain he took on himself,
p: The Hebrew has David's "afflictions"; the Greek and the Gallican Latin read "meekness."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew adflictionis eius
readings.plain: all the pain he took on himself,

readings.w: Old Greek (Codex Sinaiticus in Swete's edition, Vaticanus being lost here; Alexandrinus and the Verona and Zurich Psalters do not differ) (Psalm 131:1); Gallican Psalter mansuetudinis eius
readings.plain: all his gentleness,

why: The consonants 'nwtw can be read as 'unnoto, "his being afflicted," or as from 'anavah, "humility, meekness." The Hebrew vowels point to hardship, which fits the vow of 132:3–5. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: Her food I will surely bless;
p: The Hebrew has "her provision"; Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and the Gallican Latin have "her widow."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); a corrector of Sinaiticus and the Zurich Psalter thēran, "game" (Swete's apparatus); Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew venationem
readings.plain: Her food I will surely bless;

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (first hand) and Alexandrinus (Swete's edition, Psalm 131:15); Gallican Psalter viduam
readings.plain: Her widows I will surely bless;

why: Chēran, "widow," and thēran, "game," differ by one letter in Greek. The translator probably wrote thēran for the Hebrew tseidah, which can mean game or provision, and a copyist made it "widow," a reading that fits the "needy" in the next line. The Hebrew is followed.

a: For the LORD will judge his people
p: The Hebrew and most Greek copies have "will judge"; the first hand of Sinaiticus has "has compassion on."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); the Qumran fragment 4QPs-k (4Q92); Codex Alexandrinus, the Verona and Zurich Psalters and a corrector of Sinaiticus, from Swete's apparatus; Gallican Psalter iudicabit
readings.en: for the LORD will judge his people
readings.plain: For the LORD will judge his people

readings.w: First hand of Codex Sinaiticus (Swete's edition, Psalm 134:14)
readings.en: the LORD has compassion on his people
readings.plain: The LORD has compassion on his people

why: The line comes from Deuteronomy 32:36, where "judge" means "vindicate." The Sinaiticus scribe (or his copy) gave the sense rather than the word, and a corrector put back "will judge." The Hebrew is followed.

a: for his loyal love is forever.
p: Most Greek copies and the Gallican Latin add one more line: "Give thanks to the Lord of lords ..."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew; Codex Sinaiticus (Swete's edition, Psalm 135:26)
readings.en: for to forever (is) his loyal love
readings.plain: for his loyal love is forever.

readings.w: Old Greek in the standard editions (Rahlfs; Brenton), as reported there, ἐξομολογεῖσθε τῷ κυρίῳ τῶν κυρίων; Gallican Psalter (Psalm 135:27) confitemini Domino dominorum quoniam in aeternum misericordia eius
readings.orig: ἐξομολογεῖσθε τῷ κυρίῳ τῶν κυρίων, ὅτι εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τὸ ἔλεος αὐτοῦ
readings.en: give thanks to the Lord of lords, for his mercy is forever
readings.plain: for his loyal love is forever. / Give thanks to the Lord of lords, / for his loyal love is forever.

why: The added line repeats 136:3. It was probably added in the Greek tradition to round off the psalm, and the Gallican took it from its Greek source; the Hebrew and Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew lack it, and so does Codex Sinaiticus in Swete's edition. The Hebrew count of 26 refrains is followed. In the first line of this verse the first hand of Sinaiticus reads "the Lord of heaven"; a corrector and the other Greek witnesses have "the God of heaven," as in the Hebrew.

a: let my right hand forget.
p: The Hebrew says "let my right hand forget." The Greek and Latin have a passive; many scholars suggest "wither."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: let my right hand forget.

readings.w: Old Greek (Codex Sinaiticus in Swete's edition, Vaticanus being lost here; Alexandrinus and the Verona and Zurich Psalters do not differ) (Psalm 136:5); Gallican Psalter oblivioni detur dextera mea; Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew in oblivione sit dextera mea
readings.en: may my right hand be forgotten
readings.plain: let my right hand be forgotten.

readings.w: Modern conjecture (changing the order of two letters: tikhchash), followed by some English versions
readings.plain: let my right hand wither.

why: The Hebrew is abrupt but makes sense: the hand forgets its skill. The ancient versions read the same consonants as a passive. The conjecture has no manuscript support. The Plain keeps the Hebrew, with its word play: "If I forget you ... let my right hand forget."

a: you who will be laid waste
p: The Hebrew is passive, "the one laid waste"; the Greek has "wretched"; some modern versions change it to "destroyer."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew vastata
readings.plain: you who will be laid waste

readings.w: Old Greek (Codex Sinaiticus in Swete's edition, Vaticanus being lost here; Alexandrinus and the Verona and Zurich Psalters do not differ) (Psalm 136:8); Gallican Psalter misera
readings.plain: you wretched one

readings.w: Modern conjecture (active vowels, hashshodedah), followed by some English versions
readings.plain: you destroyer

why: The passive form speaks of Babylon's coming fate with prophetic certainty; Babylon was not laid waste when Cyrus took it in 539 BC. Some scholars think an active form, "destroyer," fits the lines that follow. No Hebrew manuscript has it, but Symmachus's Greek and the Syriac are reported to read the active form "plunderer" (BHS apparatus); the Syriac has not been checked for this part. The Greek "wretched" is a free rendering of the passive. The Hebrew is followed.

a: does not doze and does not sleep.
p: The Great Psalms Scroll from Cave 11 adds "by night" at the end of the verse.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Old Greek (Codex Sinaiticus in Swete's edition, Vaticanus being lost here; Alexandrinus and the Verona and Zurich Psalters do not differ) (Psalm 120:4)
readings.en: he does not doze and does not sleep
readings.plain: does not doze and does not sleep.

readings.w: The Great Psalms Scroll from Cave 11, 11QPs-a (11Q5)
readings.orig: לוא ינום ולוא יישן שומר ישראל בלילה
readings.en: he does not doze and does not sleep, the guard of Israel, by night
readings.plain: does not doze and does not sleep by night.

why: The added phrase anticipates "the moon in the night" of 121:6 and makes the picture of the night watchman explicit. It is not in any other witness and looks like a scribe's expansion. The Hebrew is followed.

a: life for all time.
p: Both Cave 11 Psalms scrolls end Psalm 133 with "Peace on Israel!" and lack "life."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Old Greek (Codex Sinaiticus in Swete's edition, Vaticanus being lost here; Alexandrinus and the Verona and Zurich Psalters do not differ) (Psalm 132:3)
readings.plain: life for all time.

readings.w: The Great Psalms Scroll from Cave 11, 11QPs-a (11Q5) and 11QPs-b (11Q6)
readings.en: for all time. Peace on Israel!
readings.plain: for all time. / Peace on Israel!

why: "Peace on Israel!" closes 125:5 and 128:6, and the scrolls may have brought it in to match them. The two scrolls also read "his robe" (singular) in 133:2 and "the mountain of Zion" (singular) in 133:3. The Hebrew is followed.

a: in the heavens and on the earth,
p: Three Qumran scrolls add a line: "there is none like Yah, none like the LORD, none who acts like the King of gods."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Old Greek (Codex Sinaiticus in Swete's edition, Vaticanus being lost here; Alexandrinus and the Verona and Zurich Psalters do not differ) (Psalm 134:6)
readings.en: in the heavens and on the earth
readings.plain: in the heavens and on the earth,

readings.w: The Great Psalms Scroll from Cave 11, 11QPs-a (11Q5); 4QPs-k (4Q92) and 4QPs-n (4Q95), partly restored
readings.orig: בשמים ובארץ לעשות יעשה אין כיה אין כיהוה ואין שיעשה כמלך אלוהים
readings.en: in the heavens and on the earth; he does what he does: there is none like Yah, none like the LORD, none who acts like the King of gods
readings.plain: in the heavens and on the earth. / What he does, he does: there is none like Yah, / none like the LORD, none who acts like the King of gods,

why: The three scrolls agree against the Hebrew and the Greek, so the longer text was known in more than one copy. It sharpens the comparison of 135:5 ("above every god"). Most scholars see an expansion in the style of 86:8 and Exodus 15:11. The scroll from Cave 11 also reads "our God" for "our Lord" in 135:5. The Hebrew is followed.

a: From Zion may the LORD be blessed,
p: The Hebrew blesses the LORD from Zion; the Cave 11 scroll has "May the LORD bless you from Zion," as in 134:3.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Old Greek (Codex Sinaiticus in Swete's edition, Vaticanus being lost here; Alexandrinus and the Verona and Zurich Psalters do not differ) (Psalm 134:21)
readings.en: blessed be the LORD from Zion
readings.plain: From Zion may the LORD be blessed,

readings.w: The Great Psalms Scroll from Cave 11, 11QPs-a (11Q5)
readings.en: may the LORD bless you from Zion
readings.plain: May the LORD bless you from Zion,

why: The scroll's reading repeats 134:3, which in the scroll stands far from Psalm 135. The same scroll adds to 135:2 "and exalt Yah" and "and in your midst, Jerusalem" (from 116:19). The Hebrew is followed.

a: the sun to govern the day,
p: The Cave 11 scroll has an extra line: "the sun and the moon, for his loyal love is forever."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Old Greek (Codex Sinaiticus in Swete's edition, Vaticanus being lost here; Alexandrinus and the Verona and Zurich Psalters do not differ) (Psalm 135:8)
readings.en: the sun for ruling in the day
readings.plain: the sun to govern the day,

readings.w: The Great Psalms Scroll from Cave 11, 11QPs-a (11Q5)
readings.orig: את השמש וירח כי לעולם חסדו את השמש לממשלות יום
readings.en: the sun and the moon, for his loyal love is forever; the sun to govern the day
readings.plain: the sun and the moon, for his loyal love is forever; / the sun to govern the day,

why: The extra line names the "big lights" of 136:7 before they are described, and adds a 27th refrain, so the count of 26 is not fixed in every copy. The scroll also lacks "great" in 136:4, and the fragment 4QPs-n reads "Israel his people" for "Israel his servant" in 136:22. The Hebrew is followed.
